Senses.Explanation: Literally "wild fox" (野狐) plus "Chan" (禪): "wild-fox Chan," attested 16 times in 15 allowlisted texts. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that the speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after a monk shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).
Senses.Note: The label is related by wording to the Baizhang wild-fox case (百丈野狐), but the corpus does not restrict it to citations of that case. Its verbs are openly corrective: "tear apart" (裂破), "sweep away" (掃), and "show off tricks" (逞伎倆). A verse placed under the Baizhang case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round" (修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓). The verse's own narrative language is retained as a recorded case allusion and not generalized beyond that witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方野狐禪以達磨對梁王實無功德一語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ruibai (入就瑞白禪師語錄), in Ruibai Mingxue's memorial hall address for his late teacher. Ruibai Mingxue is the exact speaker who criticizes 'wild-fox Chan from various quarters' for using Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu of Liang, 'really, no merit,' as a lineage label. Bodhidharma is the quoted case speaker whose words Ruibai discusses, not the speaker of the headword-bearing judgment.
